item.content:encoded:
Explore Index(Opens in new window)

发布源: Lowy Institute for International Policy --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-28

The 2026 Asia Power Index shows a more contested regional balance, with the gap narrowing owing more to Washington’s missteps than Beijing’s advances.

The United States and China are closer in power than at any time recorded. The gap between their military capabilities is at its narrowest since the Asia Power Index began in 2018.

US diplomatic influence underwent its largest decline on record following the Trump administration’s war with Iran and other unpopular policy decisions.

Despite a dip in relative economic capability and a year focused on internal challenges, India played a much more influential role in Asia.

Regional states demonstrated modest resilience amid geopolitical setbacks, but Indonesia’s diplomatic influence saw a particularly significant drop.

Defence cooperation between China, Russia, and North Korea accelerated in 2026, alongside closer economic ties.

These findings are drawn from the Index's measures of power across 27

countries and territories. Weigh the measures yourself, compare countries,

or follow each one across the editions.

item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
Wellbeing Government in Australia

发布源: Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-28

Improving the wellbeing of current and future generations requires a shift in mindset when it comes to what we think ofas progress.

We promote policy approaches that meet the needs of people and the environment, that are values-driven, holistic and preventative.

Seeing policy ideas through a wellbeing lens leads to decisions that reflect community values, respect environmental bounds and deploy resources more effectively for the common good.

Our vision is to embed wellbeing at the heart of Australian policymaking in a way that will lead to effective and systemic change.

Avoidable Costsis a report that addresses the substantial costs governments incur by failing to address the root causes of issues, and makes the financial case for prevention and tackling problems early.

Embedding Progressis a report from the Centre for Policy Development that provides governments with a practical manual for how to achieve better outcomes for the people they serve.

TheWellbeing Economy in Briefseries is a collection of mini briefing papers that look at the idea of a wellbeing economy, how it relates to other ideas for economic change, and what some of the core elements of a wellbeing economy are.

item.title: [Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia] Social Services Reforms
item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
Social Services Reforms

发布源: Centre for Policy Development (CPD) --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-28

In their current form, Australia’s social services are failing too many people.

Inaccessible, inconsistent, and unaffordable services are compounding inequality. Narrow eligibility criteria force people to navigate complex services or wait until they are in crisis.

From early childhood development to employment services, CPD works to change the way we deliver social services so that they truly work to support the community.

We envision a government that is more connected to communities, more hands-on, and that provides universally accessible, but not uniform, services that meet individuals’ needs.

Putting People Firstis a report that lays out a bold vision to transform social services to genuinely meet the needs of the people and communities they are designed to support.

It identifies six key drivers for reform and four practical steps governments can take now to create a system people can trust and depend on.

Growing Togetheris a report from the Centre for Policy Development’s early childhood development initiative, building on our landmarkStarting Betterreport andGuarantee for children and families.

It outlines essential steps for achieving a truly universal early education and care system.

Starting Betteris a landmark report from the Centre for Policy Development that proposes a guarantee for young children and families – a new pillar of Australia’s social deal.

Delivering the guarantee will make Australia the best place to be a child, and raise a family.

item.content:encoded:
The next Victorian government should build, build, build

发布源: Grattan Institute --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-28

by Matthew Bowes

If there’s one thing that unites Victorians during this state election, it’s pessimism. Victoria’s public debt has skyrocketed. Crime remains stubbornly high. And a plague of potholes is driving motorists to despair.

But there is one key policy issue on which Victoria has made genuine progress in recent years: Housing.

Prior to the pandemic, Melbourne had the second-most expensive average house prices in Australia, behind only Sydney. Today, Melbourne is among the nation’s most affordable cities.

The latest data from Cotality show the median Melbourne house costs about $900,000, compared to $1.4 million in Sydney, and well below average prices in Brisbane, Adelaide, Perth, and Canberra.Renters have also benefited, with rents in Melbourne growing more slowly than in other capital cities.

This didn’t happen by accident. Yes, the current national decline in house prices is mostly due to higher interest rates. But the key reason Melbourne’s housing has become more affordable is because it has built more of it.Over the past five years, Victoria has approved and built more new homes per person than any other state. Greenfield housing in Melbourne’s rapidly growing outer suburbs makes up the largest chunk of these new homes. item.content:encoded:
Fuelling the future: The Grattan Fuel Plan for Australia

发布源: Grattan Institute --Australia | 抓取时间: 2026-11-28

by Alison Reeve, Hamish McKenzie, Hayley Pring, Tony Wood

Australia has a fuel security problem. Each year, Australia uses 60 billion litres of liquid fuels – and 97 per cent of it is imported.

Australians have seen the cost of this dependency. The Iran War has cost Australians $18 billion and the federal government at least $3 billion, and has driven up inflation. In a more unstable future, disruptions like this will be more frequent.

Download the report

Download the briefing pack

Download the technical supplement

Download methodological supplement

Download the chart data

Insulating Australia from future fuel shocks requires a three-part strategy: reducing reliance, buffering impacts, and spending prudently in a crisis. In more benign times, successive federal governments mostly focused on buffers and occasional crisis spending. But Australia has no strategy to reduce reliance on imported fuels. In an era of disruption, this is no longer tenable.

The Grattan Fuel Plan for Australia is our proposal to change course.

Our centrepiece recommendation is that the government should set a sovereign fuel target for each of the largest fuel-using sectors. Road transport, mining, and aviation should use at least 50 per cent locally made fuels by 2050. To hit these targets, three moves are needed.
